title: The prince's unease
hook: the road cleared of the old and sick, yet the gods place an old man in his path (Buddhacarita 3)

segments.voice: Yesterday: life in the palace, every comfort arranged by a king afraid his son will leave. Your line: a father's fear.

Orders go out across the city. Sweep the royal road. Hang garlands. Set out banners and flowers. And one more order, the strange one: anyone old, anyone sick, anyone suffering, keep them off the road today. The prince has asked to see the gardens outside the walls, and the king, Shuddhodana, has said yes, on one condition. The world his son sees will have the hard parts taken out. By the time the chariot rolls through the gate, the street is perfect. Faces at every window. Not a single bent back in sight.
screen: `SWEEP THE ROAD. HANG GARLANDS.` → `KEEP THE OLD AND SICK AWAY.` → `A PERFECT STREET.`

segments.voice: First, the crowd. People hurry to rooftops and windows to catch sight of the prince going by, and they look at him with delight. It's a parade, and for a moment the king's plan seems to work. Second, the gap. The road has been cleared; nobody old should be there. So the poem says the gods of the pure abodes made one: an old man appears in the prince's path, bent over, white-haired, leaning on a stick. The wall the king built was solid. Something came through it anyway. Third, the question. The prince turns to his charioteer and asks what this is. The charioteer answers simply: this is old age. It takes beauty and strength and memory. This man was a child once, and grew, and this is where the years have brought him. Then the question that matters. Will this happen to me? The answer is yes. To you, and to everyone. Fourth, the unease. The prince is shaken to the core. He can't enjoy the gardens, and asks to turn back. The king's whole plan was about keeping things out. The poem's answer is that some truths don't need permission.
screen: `A CITY AT ITS WINDOWS.` · `THE GODS PLACE AN OLD MAN.` · `WILL THIS HAPPEN TO ME?` · `SOME TRUTHS DON'T NEED PERMISSION.` · then, large: `IT GETS THROUGH ANYWAY.`

segments.voice: Turn your hands over slowly and look at them as if for the first time: the lines at the knuckles, the creases of the palm, any scar, any spot. These hands were small once, and they will change again. Ask the prince's question quietly, without fear, will this happen to me, and keep breathing beside the honest answer.
old age. The charioteer's answer when the prince asks about the bent, white-haired man on the road: it takes beauty, strength and memory, and comes to everyone, the prince included. Today's word.
Your line: it gets through anyway. The road was cleared, and old age still found it. Day seven hundred one.

screen: `DAY 701 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE SICK AND THE DEAD.`

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers return to the sights of old age, sickness and death when teaching impermanence, and the scenes are painted on temple walls and told to children in Buddhist communities.

fork.setup: you're the charioteer. the prince points at an old man the king's orders should have kept away and asks what he is. what do you say?
options: tell him it's nothing, and drive on.
tell him plainly: this is old age, and it comes to everyone.
tell him to ask his father.
fork.reveal: the charioteer names it plainly, and when the prince asks if it will happen to him, says yes.

trapdoor: what you thought: the prince just happened to see an old man.
what it means: in the poem the road was cleared on purpose, and the old man appears anyway.
what a scholar hears: Ashvaghosha has the gods of the pure abodes, the shuddhavasa devas, place the sight, so the meeting becomes part of a larger turning, not an accident.

chat.says: What did the prince learn when he saw the old man on the road?
options: That aging comes to everyone, and one day it would come to him.
That the old man was a beggar the king had failed to help.
That the old man was sick, and needed a doctor right away.
chat.meaning: The charioteer names it old age: it takes beauty, strength and memory, and it comes to everyone, the prince included.

pure abodes.meaning: high heavens; in the poem their gods make the old man appear

charioteer.meaning: the prince's driver, who answers his questions

sources.ref: Buddhacarita 3 (the road cleared; the old man)

notes: All Buddhacarita material paraphrased (Cowell 1894 not on the validator list).

Confirm in Cowell canto 3: the king's order to clear the road of the afflicted; the crowds at windows and rooftops; the Shuddhadhivasa gods creating the old man; the charioteer's explanation and 'will this happen to me'; the prince's reaction (the 'thunder' simile is a paraphrase guess; Cowell may have the prince trembling 'like a bull at a thunderbolt' or similar; confirm or remove) and his turning back.
Pali spelling in the trapdoor: suddhavasa (Pali) / shuddhavasa or shuddhadhivasa (Sanskrit); confirm the form.
Some Pali commentarial tellings also have gods create the sights; the script does not claim the poem is unique in this.
